newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria unveils plans to tackle economic crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria unveils plans to tackle economic crisis.

text.p: Bulgaria's caretaker cabinet unveiled proposals on Friday aimed at rescuing the country from economic chaos.

Coping with crippling fuel shortages, stopping runs on banks, speeding up state sell-offs and resuming talks with multilateral lenders were the priorities set by interim Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski after his first day in office.
"We will begin negotiations with the European Union, the Paris Club (of official creditors) and discuss possible investment loans with the European Investment Bank," Sofianski told a news conference.
Bulgaria has been without effective government since Zhan Videnov resigned as premier and Socialist party leader on December 21.

After 30 days of mass protests fuelled by economic hardship, the discredited ex-communist majority last week gave up efforts to form a new cabinet and agreed to elections in April, 20 months before the end of their parliamentary term.

"The caretaker cabinet's success in handling the crisis will determine the success of market reforms...the next two to three months are crucial," co-director of the Institute for Liberal Studies Ivan Krastev told Reuters.
A Financial Stabilisation Council (FSC) will start talks next week with the International Monetary Fund on the introduction of a fixed exchange rate system.
On Thursday Finance Minister Svetoslav Gavriisky said Bulgaria relies entirely on external loans to repay pending foreign debt of nearly one billion dollars due this year.
"We will rely on quick privatisation deals. I hope we will be able to complete the deals already under way," said Sofianski.
Boosting privatisation revenue would enable this cash-strapped Balkan state to prop up its crumbling banks and currency.
Sofianski said he hoped to complete by end-February a $160 million deal for the sale of 60 percent in soda ash producer Sodi-Devnya to Belgian Chemical group Solvay.
A stake in Bulgaria's biggest oil refinery Neftochim will also be offered to investors.

"A drastic hike of fuel prices is urgent and the interim cabinet will discuss it on Monday," said Sofianski. Fuel shortages are threatening to paralyse Bulgaria because of insufficient cash to pay for crude supplies.

The government sent troops to enforce border controls on Friday in an attempt to curb fuel smuggling by motorists to neighbouring Yugoslavia and Macedonia, where prices are higher, said state news agency BTA. A litre of gasoline now costs 10 cents.
Fuel prices have been based on a rate of 660 levs per dollar while the lev sank to 3,000 to the dollar in the space of just one month.
The FSC is expected to come up with a project to resolve the country's enormous domestic debt, seen as a major obstacle to financial stabilisation, said Sofianski.
He assured Bulgarians that the government will under no circumstances impose a freeze on their savings and urged them to stop panic deposit withdrawal.
